      "review_date": "2022-01-16 06:07:34",
      "review_text": "Unfortunately, we came during the pre-fixed menu. There were no sides and no variety of appetizers. After reading the reviews of the food I was sad to see the menu look so bare and lonely. \nOur server was great, very friendly and the Sommelier was excellent. I chose the mushrooms, the lobster pasta and chocolate mousse. The mushrooms were hearty but the lobster pasta only had about 5 small pieces of lobster. My husband ordered the Ceasar salad, salmon and crème brûlée. He enjoyed his salad but the salmon filet was small.  With 3 (possibly small) \n items per person, you may want to grab an appetizer in the lobby bar before you come. \nIt also took forever to get each course.     },
    {
      "review_stars": 5.0,
      "review_date": "2021-12-22 22:11:03",
      "review_text": "First off, I want to say all of the staff were amazing but we loved our server Autumn. She was so sweet and really knew the menu. We ordered everything she recommended. \n\nWe got a bottle of wine to start, very crisp and light. Then for appetizers we ordered a dozen oysters which came in fresh from Baja, CA. I love that they provided a large amount of lemon, hot sauce and this amazing house made sauce. I could have eaten 100. One of the best selection of oysters we had. The quail and side salad was phenomenal. Just watch out for the little bones.\n\nFor dinner, I got the halibut which was so rich and tender I could barely scoop it up. It was very flavorful. Bae got the filet and potatoes which was cooked to perfection. We got a side of the cauliflower and it was the perfect side. \n\nWe opted for the chocolate mousse cake since chocolate is my favorite but to be honest wouldn't recommend. I wish they would expand their dessert menu but overall great night sitting by the water!"
    },
    {
      "review_stars": 4.0,
      "review_date": "2021-12-10 20:06:30",
      "review_text": "Had a great time! Good service, drinks and food. Very knowledgeable. The filet mignon was amazing and finally found a place with a good bearnaise. Lots of tarragon and saffron on the menu. Would be 5 stars with a smidge lower price tag. The lighting was a little \"shoe storey\" but maybe because we were seated in the middle of the room. We also got wine recs starting close to $300. Apart from that a great experience."
    }
  ]
}

    {
      "review_stars": 5.0,
      "review_date": "2014-08-14 04:36:40",
      "review_text": "Ordered a white cake with buttercream. When I placed the order they suggested a light lemon cream filling which I went with. It was beyond perfect. Light fluffy buttercream, moist cake, and the filling was a perfect match up. Yep, I will be back!"
    },
    {
      "review_stars": 5.0,
      "review_date": "2014-08-07 19:34:34",
      "review_text": "Katie baked the wedding cake of my dreams. It came out exactly as I wanted and was delicious. We had three tiers: two were red velvet and one was vanilla custard cake with fresh raspberries. I am very happy with our decision to choose her."
    },
    {
      "review_stars": 5.0,
      "review_date": "2014-05-09 15:00:38",
      "review_text": "Katie Teall is an ANGEL!!!  I made a wedding cake for the daughter of a very close High School friend and the Fondant I bought (FondArt) was horrible.  I spent about 7 hours kneading it and rolling it, and no matter what I did when I covered a tier of the cake it cracked.  I was so stressed that decided to go to Montecito Confections to see if I could buy Fondant there.  I got there and asked Katie Teall the sweet adorable, British owner if she could help me.  she explained that she sold the store and the rest of her Fondant was for the last 15 wedding cakes that she had to deliver during the summer.  She must have seen my face of stress, exhaustion, just lost, and asked:  How big is your cake?  I told her and she said:  Do you want me to cover it in Fondant for you?  I jumped to hug her and kiss her and hug her and kissed her some more.\n\nI came home and the mother of the bride carried the bottom tier and we went back to Montecito Confections to be saved by Katie.  We arrived and she said where is the rest of the cake?  I did not want to take advantage so we just took the biggest tier.  She said:  Bring it!\n\nHome we went after hugging Katie and kissing her some more and got help and left with two more tiers.  Katie my angel covered the three tiers!!! She was my angel.  The mother of the bride broke in tears, I guess she was worried that I was never going to serve the wedding cake.  These were tears of relief!  We ended up having the most beautiful cake and thanks to Katie.  Katie also build the cake, putting all three tiers together.  Then explained to me how to decorate it.  She told me to get a photo of the container of her fondant because she had tried all the different brands and that was the best of them all.  She said that mine was impossible to work with since it was too dry!  Katie is a walking ANGEL.  I love her, love her and love her.  All the kisses and hugs are not enough to thank her for saving the wedding cake and so much more."
    }
  ]
}

No supernatural force is required; the participants’ own bodies generate the motion, even though they often feel as if the planchette is moving “by itself.”

---

## 1. What the ideomotor effect is

| Term | Meaning |
|------|----------|
| **Ideomotor** | “Idea‑driven motor” – a motor action that is initiated by a thought or expectation rather than a conscious decision to move. |
| **Ideomotor response** | A subtle, involuntary muscle movement that occurs when a person expects or imagines a particular outcome. |

The effect was first described in the 19th‑century by psychologists such as William James and later studied in the context of dowsing, table‑turning, and spiritualist séances. When a person focuses on a particular answer (e.g., “yes” or a specific letter), the brain sends a low‑level motor signal to the hand muscles. The signal is so faint that the person does not notice it as a deliberate movement, yet it is enough to nudge the planchette.

1. **Contact points** – The board is typically played with **two or more participants** who each place a fingertip (or the pad of a finger) lightly on the planchette. For a **fair** coin each toss is independent and has probability  

\[
P(\text{Heads}) = P(\text{Tails}) = \tfrac12 .
\]

A particular sequence of 5 tosses is just the product of the probabilities of the individual outcomes that appear in that sequence.  

\[
P(\text{specific 5‑toss sequence}) = \left(\tfrac12\right)^5 = \frac1{32}.
\]

Therefore  

* \(P(\text{HHHHH}) = \left(\tfrac12\right)^5 = \frac1{32}\)  
* \(P(\text{HTTHT}) = \left(\tfrac12\right)^5 = \frac1{32}\)

Both sequences have exactly the same probability, \(1/32\) (about 3.125 %).  

So **neither sequence is more likely; they are equally likely**. The only way one sequence could be more likely than another is if the coin were biased or if we were comparing events that involve more than one specific sequence (e.g., “at least three heads”). For any single, fixed 5‑toss pattern with a fair coin, the probability is always \(1/32\).

**The “ego‑depletion” law (or “strength model of self‑control”)**

Roy Baumeister’s series of experiments in the late‑1990s and early‑2000s gave rise to what is now commonly called the **ego‑depletion effect**—the idea that self‑control operates like a limited mental resource that can become exhausted.

### Core claim
- **Self‑control draws on a finite pool of mental energy.**  
- When that pool is tapped (e.g., by resisting temptation, suppressing emotions, or performing a demanding cognitive task), the remaining capacity for subsequent self‑control tasks is reduced.
- Consequently, after an initial act of self‑control, people are more likely to give in to temptations, make impulsive choices, or perform worse on tasks that also require self‑regulation.

### Typical experimental pattern
1. **Initial “depleting” task** – participants must exert self‑control (e.g., resist eating cookies, suppress emotional expressions, or solve a difficult Stroop task).  
2. **Subsequent “target” task** – participants are then asked to perform a different self‑control‑requiring activity (e.g., persisting on a difficult puzzle, persisting on a handgrip, or making ethical decisions).  
3. **Result** – performance on the second task is systematically poorer for those who first exerted self‑control compared with a control group that performed a non‑depleting task.

### Why it’s called a “law”
- The effect was reproduced across many labs, tasks, and populations, leading researchers to treat it as a **general principle of human psychology**: *self‑control is a limited resource that can be temporarily depleted*.
- The principle has been invoked to explain a wide range of everyday phenomena—why people cheat after a hard day at work, why dieting is harder after stressful events, why willpower “fails

1. **Simplicity** – It consists of only two symbols (dot and dash) and can be sent quickly.

## 1. The Superstitious Angle: “Bad Luck”

Opening one indoors could damage delicate interiors, so the warning turned into a “bad‑luck” caution. |

| **China** | Similar to Japan—no major superstition, but people often keep umbrellas closed indoors for courtesy. | Etiquette. |
| **India** | No widespread superstition; umbrellas are simply treated as any other object. | Practicality. |

**Bottom line:** In most places the “bad luck” idea is just a cultural meme, not a literal curse. If you’re superstitious, you might feel uneasy, but nothing supernatural will happen.

---

## 2. Practical Consequences

### a. **Physical Damage**
- **Ceilings, light fixtures, and décor** – A fully opened umbrella can knock over a chandelier, dent a ceiling tile, or scratch a painted wall.
- **Furniture** – The metal ribs or the tip of the umbrella can snag upholstery or scratch wood.
- **Glass** – If you’re in a room with glass doors or windows, a sudden swing could shatter a pane.

### b. **Safety Hazards**
